chunks: Ali ibn al-Husayn, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Salim, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Amr ibn Shimir, who said:

I said to Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom, we are told in Iraq that Ali (peace be upon him) prayed over Sahl ibn Hunayf and pronounced four takbirs over him. Then he turned to those behind him and said, "He was a Badri (one who fought at Badr)."' He said, and Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'It was not so, but rather he prayed over him five times, then raised him and walked with him for a moment, then placed him down and pronounced five takbirs over him. He did that five times, until he pronounced over him five and twenty takbirs.'
And it is possible that the meaning of the report is: if the family of the deceased wish to pronounce four takbirs over him, they may leave it with their choice.

key_terms.بَدْرِيّاً: Badri (one who participated in the Battle of Badr)

ai.seo_question: What is the unique method of performing funeral prayer described in this hadith regarding Sahl ibn Hunayf?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq clarifies a historical discrepancy regarding the funeral prayer of Sahl ibn Hunayf, revealing that Imam Ali performed a unique, extended ritual of twenty-five takbirs by raising and lowering the body, rather than the standard four. This detail highlights the flexibility (rukhsah) in Shia jurisprudence, where the Imam’s specific practice serves as a precedent for mourners to either follow the elaborate method or adhere to the common four-takbir format. The hadith underscores the scholarly emphasis on distinguishing between the Prophet’s/Imams' specific actions and general communal practices.
